title: Configuration Belongs to Its Reach
hints: Choose the owner of a configuration value by where the value may differ, not by which extension reads it.

hints.text: A value that may differ per site belongs to the site's settings. A set declares its key, type and default in Configuration/Sets/<Set>/settings.definitions.yaml; the site can override it in config/sites/<site>/settings.yaml.

hints: Extension configuration is installation-wide. Define there only a value that is genuinely one per TYPO3 installation, and read it through ExtensionConfiguration rather than accessing TYPO3_CONF_VARS['EXTENSIONS'] directly.

A scheduler task's own parameters belong to that task instance. Expose them as fields when the task is configured and persist them with the task instead of turning one task's choice into site or installation configuration.

title: What TYPO3 Reads From the Environment
hints: Three environment variables reach TYPO3 with no project code behind them, and SystemEnvironmentBuilder is the only thing that reads them: TYPO3_CONTEXT selects the application context, TYPO3_PATH_ROOT names the document root and TYPO3_PATH_APP the project root above it. Each is also accepted with a REDIRECT_ prefix, which is what a web server forwards into FastCGI, and the context additionally as HTTP_TYPO3_CONTEXT for Apache suexec. No other key of TYPO3_CONF_VARS has an environment variable behind it.

Everything else a deployment takes from the environment is the project's own getenv() in config/system/additional.php: the encryption key, the database credentials, the trusted-host pattern, the mail transport. No running installation picks up TYPO3_ENCRYPTION_KEY or TYPO3_DB_HOST by itself — $GLOBALS['TYPO3_CONF_VARS']['SYS']['encryptionKey'] = getenv('TYPO3_ENCRYPTION_KEY'); is the line that makes that variable exist, and a readme documenting the name without such a line documents nothing. TYPO3 also ships no .env reader, so whatever puts a .env file into the process environment — DDEV, the container runtime, a dotenv component the project required — is the project's choice as well.

hints.text: Setting the encryption key from an extension's ext_localconf.php stops working. The empty-key check moved ahead of extension loading in the bootstrap, so the installation throws "TYPO3 Encryption is empty" before the assignment is ever evaluated. Both config/system/settings.php and config/system/additional.php are evaluated before that check, and reading the variable there is the migration.

hints: A repository whose .gitignore lists .env has promised a reader nothing in TYPO3 provides, and symfony/dotenv is the usual one: loadEnv() reads the file and populates $_ENV and $_SERVER only. getenv() — the form config/system/additional.php reads a variable in — answers false until usePutenv() has been called on the Dotenv instance, which is off by default, so the file parses and configures nothing.

loadEnv() leaves a variable that is already in the process environment alone, which is what lets a real environment variable beat the committed file; overrideExistingVars inverts that and a deployment does not want it.
Where a placeholder is written instead is environment-placeholders, and what reads the environment while it runs is environment-runtime-readers.

title: %env() in a YAML Configuration
hints: %env(NAME)% is a YAML placeholder resolved by the core's YamlFileLoader, not a configuration syntax that holds everywhere, and it throws when the variable is unset rather than falling back. It reaches what that loader reads — a site's config.yaml and settings.yaml, the form framework's YAML, an RTE preset — and config/services.yaml resolves the same spelling through Symfony's own container, where the TYPO3: prefix additionally exposes Environment methods rather than the process environment. It does not reach config/system/settings.php or additional.php, which are plain PHP that no YAML loader sees.

A placeholder already in a site configuration survives the backend module but cannot be introduced there. The module loads config.yaml with imports processed and placeholders left alone, so the raw %env(NAME)% is what is edited, and SiteWriter runs YamlPlaceholderGuard over what comes back, which refuses a placeholder that was not in the file before. A value taken from the environment is therefore put into config.yaml by hand.

title: What Reads the Environment While It Runs
hints: Two console commands do read a fixed set of variables, and only while they run. typo3 setup accepts the TYPO3_DB_ family (DRIVER, HOST, PORT, USERNAME, PASSWORD, DBNAME), the TYPO3_SETUP_ family for the administrator and the site to create, plus TYPO3_PROJECT_NAME and TYPO3_SERVER_TYPE, as answers to the questions it would otherwise ask; typo3 backend:user:create accepts the TYPO3_BE_USER_ family the same way. Ask the command's --help for the exact set, because it has grown between majors. What setup does with those values is write settings.php once, which is why a project can set TYPO3_DB_HOST, watch the installation come up, and still have nothing that reads the variable afterwards.

TypoScript reaches the environment in two places that are easy to miss when auditing what a site depends on: the constant function modifier := getEnv(NAME), and getenv as a getData key, so data = getenv:NAME resolves in stdWrap. Both read the environment of the process serving the request, which is not the shell a deployment script ran in.

title: What typo3 setup Takes and What It Refuses
hints: The command takes a connection type and writes a driver name, and the two spellings differ. --driver and TYPO3_DB_DRIVER accept mysqli, mysqliSocket, pdoMysql, pdoMysqlSocket, postgres or sqlite; config/system/settings.php then carries the DBAL driver behind it, so sqlite is persisted as pdo_sqlite and postgres as pdo_pgsql. Handing the persisted name back is refused with exception 1669905551, saying that connection type does not exist — the file the command wrote is not a source for the option that wrote it.

sqlite is the connection type that needs nothing else. No host, port, dbname, username or password is read for it, and the file is calculated rather than named: var/sqlite/cms-<random>.sqlite where the project root sits above the document root, the config directory where it does not. The name is random per run, so a second run behind --force points settings.php at a new empty database and leaves the first file on disk.

It refuses a database that already has tables, with exception 1669747200 naming how many it found; --force overwrites the settings files and never the schema. That check is on the server-database path only — the sqlite path calculates a fresh file and never reaches it. Without --force the run stops earlier still, on config/system/settings.php already existing, which is exception 1669747685 and which --no-interaction answers with no. So the guard an idempotent installer needs is that file: test for it yourself rather than reading an exit code.

An uncaught exception ends the run as the command's usage synopsis and exit status 255, whatever it was about. That surface is symfony/console and not TYPO3: renderThrowable prints the running command's synopsis for every throwable, and run() clamps an exit code above 255 to exit status 255, which every nine-digit TYPO3 exception code lands on. So a synopsis says nothing about the arguments, and the message printed above it is the whole of the cause.

--admin-user-password and TYPO3_SETUP_ADMIN_PASSWORD are validated against the policy named in BE/passwordPolicy, whose default asks for eight characters carrying an upper case letter, a lower case letter, a digit and a special character. A value that misses one stops the run with exception 1669747614, Administrator password not secure enough, listing what it missed. The check runs after the database has been imported, so the schema is already written when it stops: on a server database the next attempt is refused by the table check that --force does not clear, and on sqlite a fresh file is calculated instead.
--create-site <url> and TYPO3_SETUP_CREATE_SITE create the root page and its site configuration under config/sites/.

The config.yaml it writes carries errorHandling and routes as empty flow mappings, errorHandling: {  } with the two spaces symfony/yaml renders an empty array with, because that file is dumped without the flag that would write an empty sequence instead. An edit looking for the key on a line of its own, with its entries below it, matches neither.

hints.text: dependencies is written the same way and is empty unless typo3/fluid-styled-content is active, which an extension repository's installation commonly is not. Where it is active the key carries that set and typo3/fluid-styled-content-css.

The same run writes config/sites/<identifier>/setup.typoscript, a welcome page = PAGE with the TYPO3 logo and the content of the root page in it. A site's own TypoScript is applied after the sets it depends on — SysTemplateTreeBuilder hangs the set includes below the site's include node, and a node's own lines are read after its children — so the file replaces every path it assigns and leaves the rest of what the sets built standing. An installation whose rendering comes from a set deletes that file or replaces its content.

That override is silent: the page answers HTTP 200, the log stays empty, and the set really is loaded. What tells it apart from a set that was never applied is a marker on a path the welcome file does not assign — a page.5 = TEXT added to the set renders in the first case and is missing in the second.
The command inserts a root sys_template row instead, titled Main TypoScript Rendering, carrying clear = 3 and the same welcome page object in its config, and it writes no site TypoScript file.

That row is the harder collision, because a sys_template that clears resets the AST: a site carrying sets loses everything they contributed rather than the paths the row itself names. The same clash inside a functional test is extension-test-site.

Neither that pair nor --distribution is read where a distribution is already active, and shipping Initialisation/data.xml or Initialisation/data.t3d is the whole test for being one. In Composer mode every required package is active, so requiring such a package makes both inert: the command warns that they have no effect, writes no site configuration, and the installation has no way to be told its own URL.

--distribution names a package whose content is imported instead. It needs typo3/cms-impexp active and may not be combined with --create-site, which is exception 1775034289. What imports the distribution is the package initialisation setup triggers as its last step — sitepackage-initial-content.

hints: Under DDEV the variables ride in on the command itself: ddev exec TYPO3_DB_DRIVER=mysqli TYPO3_SETUP_ADMIN_USERNAME=admin vendor/bin/typo3 setup --no-interaction sets them for that run, because ddev exec joins its arguments into one line and hands that line to bash inside the container. There is no --env option to reach for, and asking for one is refused for an unknown shorthand flag; the flags are --dir, --service, --user, --quiet and --raw. --raw is what takes the bash away, and typing it at all is what does it: --raw, --raw=true and --raw=false behave alike, the arguments are then handed to the container as they stand, and the assignment is looked for as a program with "executable file not found in $PATH". Its own help says the flag defaults to true, and the default nevertheless interprets with bash.

That bash reads every argument, so anything it acts on is spent before TYPO3 sees it: a parenthesis in a regular expression stops the run as a syntax error, and --filter A|B loses its pipe to a pipeline. A value with a space is the quieter one — DDEV quotes such an argument as it builds the line, a quoted word is no assignment to bash, and TYPO3_PROJECT_NAME=Two Words becomes a command name that is not found. ddev exec bash -c 'TYPO3_PROJECT_NAME="Two Words" vendor/bin/typo3 setup --no-interaction' is the form that carries all of them, because the quoting is then inside a string bash alone reads.

A line break survives that join where the quotes around it do not: DDEV wraps the whole argument in double quotes, so a newline reaches the container's bash as a newline. A backslash immediately before it is a line continuation there, so a command written across several lines runs as the same command on one line does. A line that ends without one ends the command, and every assignment above the break is spent on a command of its own — what reaches TYPO3 is the last line with its values missing, which comes back as the usage synopsis rather than as a shell error. A backslash with a space after it is that same break, and bash reports the space as a command that is not found.

web_environment in the project's .ddev/config.yaml is a different set of variables, and an extension repository commonly carries typo3DatabaseHost, typo3DatabaseName, typo3DatabaseUsername and typo3DatabasePassword there against a database named t3func. That is the family a functional test run reads, which is project-extension-tests, and setup reads none of it. So those lines in a file the caller is reading anyway say the container is configured for the tests, not that the installation is ready to be created.
Which TYPO3_ variables the command reads, and why nothing reads them once it has run, is environment-runtime-readers.

title: The Install Tool Password Is a Value of Its Own
hints: The install tool password and a backend user's password are two values. typo3 setup sets both from the one value it was handed. backend:resetpassword and the backend change the user's password alone, so the install tool still opens with the old value. A question about the administrator password therefore owes the install tool password in the same answer.

hints.text: install:password:set changes the install tool password. It asks for the password and generates one where the answer is empty, and it writes the hash to BE/installToolPassword in config/system/settings.php. It fails where additional.php overrides that value, because a change in settings.php would have no effect there.

hints: Every covered line accepts the hash by hand. Enter the new password at the install tool login. The refusal says "Given password does not match the install tool login password. Calculated hash:" and carries the hash. Write that hash into BE/installToolPassword in config/system/settings.php.

The hash travels with the committed config/system/settings.php. Where an agent chose or printed the password, anybody who holds that value opens the install tool of every environment the repository reaches. Change the password before the project is deployed or public, or keep the value out of settings.php as project-configuration-files states.

hints.text: The install tool has four backend modules under System: /module/system/maintenance, /module/system/settings, /module/system/upgrade and /module/system/environment. /typo3/install and /typo3/install.php redirect to /?__typo3_install, the standalone form, which needs the ENABLE_INSTALL_TOOL file and the install tool password.

The install tool has four backend modules under Admin Tools: /module/tools/maintenance, /module/tools/settings, /module/tools/upgrade and /module/tools/environment. /typo3/install.php is the standalone form, which needs the ENABLE_INSTALL_TOOL file and the install tool password.

hints: Those modules declare access systemMaintainer and sudo mode. In the Development context every administrator passes. In another context a non-empty SYS/systemMaintainers admits the users it lists and nobody else, so an administrator outside the list sees none of the modules. typo3 setup adds the administrator it creates to that list.
